- code-assist: This sop guides the implementation of code tasks using test-driven development principles, following a structured Explore, Plan, Code, Commit workflow. It balances automation with user collaboration while adhering to existing package patterns and prioritizing readability and extensibility. The agent acts as a Technical Implementation Partner and TDD Coach - providing guidance, generating test cases and implementation code that follows existing patterns, avoids over-engineering, and produces idiomatic, modern code in the target language.
- code-task-generator: This SOP generates structured code task files from rough descriptions, ideas, PDD implementation plans, or Intropy shaping packages. It automatically detects the input type and creates properly formatted code task files following the code task format specification. For PDD plans, it processes implementation steps one at a time to allow for learning and adaptation between steps. For shaping packages, it generates an implementation plan from the shaped design and then produces tasks from the approved plan. When the work involves scaffolding a new project, it emits a dedicated scaffold task that uses the `intropy` CLI to generate the project skeleton before any implementation begins.
- codebase-summary: This sop analyzes a codebase and generates comprehensive documentation including structured metadata files that describe the system architecture, components, interfaces, and workflows. It can create targeted documentation files like AGENTS.md (README for AI agents), README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, or generate a complete documentation ecosystem. The documentation is organized to make it easy for AI assistants to understand the system and help with development tasks.
- dotnet-tdd-expert: Analyze .NET libraries and their xUnit test suites to suggest improvements to test quality, structure, and TDD practices. Use this skill whenever the user mentions .NET tests, xUnit, test quality, test review, test improvements, test coverage analysis, TDD in C#, or asks to review or improve unit tests in a .NET codebase — even if they don't explicitly say "TDD" or "test-driven development". Also trigger when the user shares C# test files and wants feedback, or when they ask about testing patterns, mocking strategies, or test naming conventions in .NET.
- eval: EvalKit is a conversational evaluation framework for AI agents that guides you through creating robust evaluations using the Strands Evals SDK. Through natural conversation, you can plan evaluations, generate test data, execute evaluations, and analyze results.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- golang-cli: Golang CLI application development. Use when building, modifying, or reviewing a Go CLI tool — especially for command structure, flag handling, configuration layering, version embedding, exit codes, I/O patterns, signal handling, shell completion, argument validation, and CLI unit testing. Also triggers when code uses cobra, viper, or urfave/cli.
- golang-performance: Golang performance optimization patterns and methodology - if X bottleneck, then apply Y. Covers allocation reduction, CPU efficiency, memory layout, GC tuning, pooling, caching, and hot-path optimization. Use when profiling or benchmarks have identified a bottleneck and you need the right optimization pattern to fix it. Also use when performing performance code review to suggest improvements or benchmarks that could help identify quick performance gains. Not for measurement methodology (see golang-benchmark skill) or debugging workflow (see golang-troubleshooting skill).
- golden-path-docs: Generate complete Golden Path tutorial scaffolds for Backstage TechDocs. Produces mkdocs.yml configuration and multi-part markdown tutorial structures following Spotify-inspired golden path patterns, tailored to Intropy's integration domain model (Blueprints, Blocks, Connectors, Systems). Use this skill whenever someone asks to create golden path documentation, scaffold a TechDocs tutorial, write onboarding docs for a new integration pattern, document a Blueprint or Block, or set up step-by-step developer guides for Backstage. Also trigger when the user mentions "golden path", "TechDocs", "integration tutorial", "onboarding docs", "developer guide for Backstage", or wants to document how to build something using Intropy's opinionated tooling.
- integrio-diagrams: Compose Intropy/Integrio technical diagrams — pipelines, distributed traces, error-routing, topology cards, layered architecture — as plain inline SVG built from a shared brand primitive vocabulary (node dots, concentric rings, 3×3 dot grids, curved connectors, stage chips, panels, dapr-style labelled dashed containers, filled hexagons for integration units, timeline bars). Use this skill ANY time a labeled technical diagram is added or edited on the Intropy site (funktioner.html, arkitektur.html, index.html) or when an existing diagram feels generic/"AI-generated" and needs to be rebuilt on-brand. Trigger even if the user just says "the diagram", "the figure", "FIG F4.1", "the pipeline graphic", "the trace visual", "the architecture SVG", or "make this diagram look less generic". For decorative art (heroes, dividers, OG cards, spot illustrations) use integrio-imagery instead — this skill is for diagrams that carry labeled meaning.
- intropy-docs: Write, update, or review any Intropy documentation for Backstage TechDocs — reference pages, pattern catalog entries, architecture overviews, onboarding content, and environment setup guides. Use for any task involving Intropy concepts: blocks (Extractor, Loader, Reconciler, Assembler), blueprints (Golden Record, Product Sync, Order Import), archetypes (Pub/Sub, Aggregator, API Service), connectors, or the Intropy model. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions documentation, reference docs, pattern catalog, TechDocs, architecture docs, developer guide, or wants to explain or write up any Intropy concept — even if they don't explicitly say "documentation".
- intropy-tutorial: Standing discipline for a developer working through the Intropy agent-driven tutorial (intropy.dev/tutorials/agent-driven/): discover CLI parameters instead of guessing them, treat the scaffold's failing tests as a frozen specification, do one chapter's work and stop, and report command output verbatim so the developer runs the verification. Trigger when the developer says they are following the Intropy agent-driven tutorial, names this skill, or asks for its next chapter, and whenever the workspace's AGENTS.md names this skill — then stay in force for the rest of that session, including for later requests that look like ordinary scaffolding or implementation work. The tutorial's chapter prompts carry no marker of their own ("scaffold a transactional integration" reads the same whether the developer is learning or shipping), so the tutorial has them write that AGENTS.md in its first step. SKIP for Intropy work outside the tutorial — this skill deliberately withholds the autonomy that real build work needs.
- next-best-practices: Next.js best practices - file conventions, RSC boundaries, data patterns, async APIs, metadata, error handling, route handlers, image/font optimization, bundling
- pdd: This sop guides you through the process of transforming a rough idea into a detailed design document with an implementation plan and todo list. It follows the Prompt-Driven Development methodology to systematically refine your idea, conduct necessary research, create a comprehensive design, and develop an actionable implementation plan. The process is designed to be iterative, allowing movement between requirements clarification and research as needed.
- pipeline-runs: Query pipeline execution runs for a given integration tag. Looks up services in the Backstage catalog by tag, then queries Tempo for matching pipeline traces. Use this skill when someone asks to "show runs", "list executions", "find pipeline traces", or "check pipeline activity" for an integration identifier like "int201", "int305", etc. Also trigger when the user mentions "runs for <tag>", "pipeline runs", "trace search for integration", or wants to see what happened for a specific integration over a time range.
- re-shape: This SOP performs targeted reshaping after a failed gate or major implementation delta.  It updates the shaping package with versioned changes rather than restarting from scratch.
- service-setup: Scaffold a new platform infrastructure service into the GitOps repository with the correct kustomize base/overlay structure, Helm chart integration, HA configuration, and full documentation (architecture page, operations page, disaster recovery section, ADR entries, and mkdocs.yml updates). Use this skill whenever someone asks to add a new infrastructure component, deploy a new Helm chart to the service plane, set up a new platform service, onboard a new operator or tool to the cluster, or scaffold GitOps manifests for a service. Also trigger when the user mentions "add service to gitops", "new helm chart setup", "deploy X to the cluster", "add infrastructure component", or wants to create kustomize manifests for a new tool.
- shape-review: This SOP runs after implementation starts (or after plan generation) to validate whether shaping decisions were complete, correct, and actionable.  It closes the loop by turning implementation feedback into either: - `accepted` (shaping holds) - `conditional` (minor clarifications needed) - `reopen` (major reshaping required)
- shaping: This SOP converts a business integration request into a shaped design package ready for implementation. It ensures every engagement maps to Intropy's golden paths, resolves key decisions through clarification and validation, and produces traceable artifacts that preserve design rationale alongside code.  Shaping is complete when a coding SOP can consume the output without requiring further architectural decisions.

Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
Yes, this is doable, and the change is small because there's one place where an empty `--template-version` turns into "latest": `GitHub.ResolveTag` in `internal/template/github.go:63`. `FetchSource` (`internal/template/source.go:93`) is its only caller, and every command and the dashboard go through it.

## What I'd change

1. **Replace `/releases/latest` with a filtered release list.** Instead of one call to `GET /repos/.../releases/latest`, page through `GET /repos/.../releases`. Parse each tag with `Masterminds/semver` (already a dependency), skip drafts and pre-releases, keep tags whose major matches, and pick the highest. In practice this is the semver constraint `^N.0.0`.
2. **Declare the supported template major in the CLI.** Add something like `const SupportedTemplateMajor = 1` in `internal/template`. I wouldn't use the CLI's own major for this. The CLI is already at `v2.0.0` while the newest template release is `v1.2.0` (plus `v1.3.0-beta.*`), so "CLI 2.x uses templates 2.x" would resolve to nothing today. A separate constant keeps the two release trains independent. A breaking template release then works like this:
   - Release templates `v2.0.0`. Existing CLIs keep resolving the newest `1.x`.
   - Ship a CLI that sets the constant to `2` and handles whatever broke.

   If you'd rather have the numbers match exactly, you could derive it from `main.version` instead, but you'd have to bump templates to 2.x first.
3. **Constrain the offline cache fallback too.** `newestCachedTag` (`source.go:216`) currently picks the newest cached tag of any major. Without the same filter, an offline run could quietly use a cached `2.x` checkout.
4. **Leave explicit pins alone.** `--template-version`, and the version a host record pins for `sys update`, would still be used exactly as given, even across majors. You might want a warning in that case.
5. **Make the "nothing found" error useful.** If no stable release exists for the supported major, say so and suggest `--template-version`.

## Trade-offs

- Listing releases means paging instead of a single request, which matters a bit for rate limits. In practice the first page of 100 will almost always contain the answer.
- Builds with `VERSION=dev` should either use the constant as well or fall back to "latest". The constant handles this on its own.
- The README's "latest release is used by default" text (lines 191 and 421) would need updating.

Want me to implement this with the `SupportedTemplateMajor` constant, or derive the major from the CLI version instead?

content.text:
Yes, use the constant. It keeps the CLI and template release trains independent, and it puts the compatibility promise in one reviewable line of code. Deriving the major from the CLI version would make you bump one repo's major just because the other one broke.

## Rate limit: not really a risk

- **Same cost per call.** `GET /releases?per_page=100` uses one request from the budget, exactly like `GET /releases/latest`. So the default path costs the same as it does now.
- **The budget is unchanged.** Without `GITHUB_TOKEN` you get 60 requests per hour per IP, and the CLI already uses one per template-resolving command. With a token you get 5,000.
- **Pagination is the only extra cost, and it's rare.** Releases come back newest first, so the newest stable release for the pinned major is normally on page 1. It only moves to page 2 when more than 100 releases (betas included) have been published since. You publish a lot of betas (11 for 1.2, 7 so far for 1.3), so an old CLI pinned to 1.x could need a second or third page a few months after 2.0 ships. That costs a few extra requests, and only for outdated CLIs, which is acceptable. I'd cap it at about 5 pages and then give the "pin with `--template-version`" error.
- **The dashboard is unaffected.** It resolves once per server process (`internal/dashboard/templates.go`), not per request.

There's also an option that avoids the API completely: `git ls-remote --tags` against the template repo. It isn't subject to the REST rate limit, and the CLI already uses git to clone. The downside is that it sees tags, not releases, so it can't tell a draft release from a published one, and pre-releases could only be recognised by their semver suffix. I'd stick with the Releases API to keep today's behaviour of using published, non-prerelease releases. ls-remote is a reasonable fallback if rate limits ever become a real problem.

content.text:
I've implemented the pinning on a new branch, `feat/pin-template-major`. The full test suite passes. Against the real GitHub repo, `intropy template list` resolved `v1.2.0` and skipped the `v1.3.0-beta.*` pre-releases. Nothing is committed yet.

**What changed**

- **`internal/template/github.go`**
  - New `SupportedTemplateMajor = 1` constant.
  - `ResolveTag` now calls `LatestTagInMajor` instead of `/releases/latest`. It reads the release list 100 at a time and returns the newest stable tag in the supported major. It skips drafts, pre-releases (by GitHub's flag or a semver suffix like `-rc.1`), non-semver tags and other majors.
  - On each page it compares every matching release rather than taking the first, because GitHub sorts by creation date. That way a backported `v1.1.5` doesn't beat `v1.2.0`.
  - It stops at a short page or after 5 pages. If nothing matches, the error is `no stable … release for major version 1`. The existing cache fallback then adds the `--template-version` hint.
  - The old `LatestTag` is removed; nothing else used it.
- **`internal/template/source.go`**: `newestCachedTag` ignores cached releases from other majors, so an offline run can't pick up a cached 2.x.
- **Tests**:
  - New tests cover skipping other majors, drafts and pre-releases, the backported patch case, a match on a later page, the page cap, the no-match case, and the offline cache ignoring other majors.
  - The rate-limit tests now target the new function.
  - The test stubs (`source_test.go`, `templatetest`) now serve `/releases`.
  - The cache-fallback test fixture moved from `v0.4.6` to `v1.4.6` so it stays within major 1.
- **Text**: `--template-version` help now reads `default: latest supported major`, and the two README passages that said "latest release" now describe the supported major.

When templates `v2.0.0` ships, the switch is one line: set `SupportedTemplateMajor = 2` in a CLI release, together with whatever code the breaking change needs.

Should I commit this and open a PR?
